passages.judgement: A clear gain over the current text. The mis-glosses it fixes are real and well sourced: hurricanoes, thought-executing, court holy-water, knave, spill, high-engender'd battles and scanted courtesy. One ear-trap needs fixing (11.4). The rest are optional refinements. The current was better in two small respects: bare 'grace' in 11.8, and the famous wording of 11.12.

findings.original: Crack nature’s moulds, all germens spill at once, / That make ingrateful man!
findings.proposed_text: Crack the molds that nature casts us in, and spill and destroy at once all the seeds that make ungrateful man!
findings.issue: Glossing 'moulds' so that no listener hears fungus is right, but 'us' adds a first-person frame. Nature's moulds are the forms in which nature shapes all creatures (Theobald in Furness: 'Crack nature's mould and spill all the seeds of matter that are hoarded within it'). The curse is on the whole creation, not only on 'us'. 'spill and destroy' is a sound gloss (Steevens in Furness; Schmidt spill 2, citing this line). The reason's 'flattened double sense' overstates it, since the primary sense here is 'destroy'.
findings.fix: Crack the molds in which nature shapes all life, and spill and destroy at once all the seeds that make ungrateful man!

findings.proposed_text: forerunners of the thunderbolts that split oaks,
findings.issue: 'forerunners' is correct (Schmidt; Cotgrave via Wright in Furness). But the reason treats the current 'advance guards' as a military intrusion to be replaced. Steevens (Furness) says the word 'originally meant the foremost scouts of an army', and the martial colour prepares the 'battles' of 11.3. Either wording is acceptable.
findings.fix: No text change needed; correct the reason. To keep the military image: 'the scouts that race ahead of the thunderbolts that split oaks'.

findings.issue: Heard aloud, 'how many beggars' first parses as a quantity ('that is the number of beggars who marry'). That is an unintended ambiguity in a narrated text. The intended sense is Mason's 'so many beggars marry', i.e. this is the way many beggars marry (Furness, New Variorum King Lear (1880)).
findings.fix: that's the way many beggars marry.

findings.original: Marry, here’s grace and a codpiece; that’s a wise man and a fool.
findings.proposed_text: Why, here's His Grace and a codpiece; that's a wise man and a fool.
findings.issue: Making the royal title audible is right (Steevens in Furness: 'the king's grace' was the usual expression). But the change swaps one sense for the other. Plain 'grace' also carries its everyday sense of virtue (Schmidt grace 9), which pairs naturally against the lewd codpiece. The current kept that sense and the proposal drops it. Also, in present-day usage 'His Grace' is the style of a duke or archbishop, so a listener may not hear the King.
findings.fix: Why, here's grace — His Grace the King — and a codpiece; that's a wise man and a fool.

findings.original: Such sheets of fire, such bursts of horrid thunder,
findings.proposed_text: such sheets of fire, such bursts of dreadful thunder,
findings.issue: The gloss is correct (Schmidt: horrid 'dreadful, shocking, hideous', citing this line). But Shakespeare saves 'dreadful' for Lear's next speech ('this dreadful pudder', 'these dreadful summoners'). The proposal now has three uses of 'dreadful' in quick succession and loses Kent's own word.
findings.fix: such sheets of fire, such bursts of hideous thunder,

findings.original: That under covert and convenient seeming / Hast practis’d on man’s life:
findings.proposed_text: you who have plotted against a man's life behind a hidden, respectable front.
findings.issue: 'covert ... seeming' is a disguising appearance (Schmidt covert: 'secret, hid, disguised'). The front conceals the plotter; it is not itself hidden. 'a hidden, respectable front' is therefore slightly self-contradictory by ear.
findings.fix: you who have plotted against a man's life behind a disguise of respectability.

findings.original: The art of our necessities is strange, / That can make vile things precious.
findings.proposed_text: Our need has a strange art: it can make vile things precious.
findings.issue: The rewrite is clear and faithful, but this is one of the play's best-known lines. Only the relative 'That' is hard by ear, and rule 2 favours keeping such lines recognizable. A colon fixes the parse without rewording. 'vile' is kept in Schmidt's old sense 'low, mean', which the context carries.
findings.fix: The art of our necessities is strange: it can make vile things precious.

current_defects_confirmed: 11.1: 'hurricanes' mis-glosses 'hurricanoes' (waterspouts: Dyce in Furness; Schmidt, citing this line and Troil. V, 2, 172).
11.1: 'thought-swift' keeps the speed and drops the killing of 'thought-executing' (Johnson in Furness; Schmidt, citing this line).
11.1: 'spill all seeds' loses spill = destroy (Steevens in Furness; Schmidt spill 2, citing this line). 'cataracts' and 'thick rotundity' are left as hard Latinate words.
11.2: 'holy water at court' takes the idiom literally. 'court holy-water' means flattery, fair words (Steevens, and Malone citing Cotgrave, in Furness; Schmidt).
11.3: 'let fall your horrible pleasure', 'servile ministers' and 'high-engendered battles' are left untranslated (battle = army, Schmidt battle 3; high-engendered, Schmidt citing this line).
11.4: the head-piece double sense is flattened. The codpiece and toe/heart quatrains stay opaque ('both the head and he shall have lice', 'of a corn, cry woe').
11.8: bare 'grace' hides the royal title (Steevens in Furness), though it does keep the virtue sense.
11.9: 'horrid' has weakened in current English, and 'I do not remember ever to have heard' is stilted.

11.10: 'undivulged', 'Caitiff', 'convenient seeming', 'Close pent-up guilts' and 'rive' are left untranslated (the Schmidt entries cite this passage). Persons are mixed in 'you wretch, who has within you'.
11.11: 'some shelter' drops the personified 'friendship', 'go to this hard house ... return' is broken syntax, and 'stinted courtesy' is opaque (Schmidt scant vb. 2, citing this line).
11.12: 'Poor fool and knave' is heard as 'rogue', though 'knave' is a term of endearment here (Schmidt knave 1, citing III, 2, 72). 'sorry yet' is archaic.
current_defects_disputed: 11.1 (defect list): 'British moulds in an otherwise American-spelled edition' is inaccurate. The live king-lear-modern-en edition mixes spellings: honour 9 / honor 9, favour 7 / favor 5, colour 5 / color 0, labour 4 / labor 1, sulphur 2 / sulfur 0. Moving to American spelling is a house-style choice, not a fix of an outlier. The Hamlet edition cited as precedent uses American spelling (honor, favor) but contains neither 'molds' nor 'sulfurous'.
11.1 (reasons): the current 'advance guards' is not a mis-rendering. Steevens (Furness) gives 'foremost scouts of an army' as the word's original sense.
11.12: 'The art of our necessities left hard to parse by ear' is only partly right. The difficulty is the relative 'That', and the famous wording can be kept (see finding).
current_better: 11.8: bare 'grace' kept the virtue sense that 'His Grace' drops. Combine both (see finding).
11.12: the current kept the famous wording 'The art of our necessities is strange'. Keep it with a colon (see finding).
11.1: 'advance guards' kept the martial sense of vaunt-courier (Steevens). The proposed 'forerunners' is equally acceptable.

passages.judgement: Clearly better. It corrects two outright mis-glosses in the song ('owe' = own, 'in-a-door' = at home), glosses coxcomb, brach and motley at first mention, and lands the monopoly, egg and 'like myself' jokes. All findings are optional notes. The one thing the current did better is the archaic 'sirrah', which kept Lear's rebuke distinct from his affectionate 'boy'.

findings.original: How now, my pretty knave, how dost thou?
findings.proposed_text: Well, my pretty lad, how are you doing?
findings.issue: The gloss is right (Schmidt knave 1, a term of endearment). But the cited location 'I, 4, 46' comes from a garbled extract. Schmidt's printed entry reads 'where's my k., my fool? I, 4, 46. now, my friendly k., I thank thee, 103. my pretty k. 107.'
findings.fix: Cite Schmidt, knave 1), 'my pretty k.', Lr. I, 4, 107.

findings.original: Take heed, sirrah, the whip. / When were you wont to be so full of songs, sirrah? / An you lie, sirrah, we’ll have you whipped.
findings.proposed_text: Take heed, boy — the whip. / When did you start being so full of songs, boy? / If you lie, boy, we'll have you whipped.
findings.issue: Translating 'sirrah' is right. But in this same passage plain 'boy' is Lear's affectionate address to the Fool: 4.69 'Why, my boy?', 4.79 'Why, no, boy', 4.87 'Do you call me fool, boy?'. White (Furness) notes that Lear always addresses the Fool with terms of endearment. Using 'boy' for his three 'sirrah's erases the switch to a master's rebuke. The reason says 'boy' without 'my' carries the rebuke, but 4.79 and 4.87 contradict that. The threats of the whip still carry the tone, so the proposal is acceptable as it stands.
findings.fix: Optional: a curt master's 'sir' ('Take heed, sir — the whip.' / 'When did you start being so full of songs, sir?' / 'If you lie, sir, we'll have you whipped.'). Otherwise keep 'boy' and accept the loss.

findings.proposed_text: at dice stake less than you throw for;
findings.issue: This is a crux. Furness records Mrs Griffiths ('never set equal to the stake you throw for'), whom the proposal follows. He also records Schmidt's two readings: 'set a less sum than thou hast won by thy last throw', and 'keep on throwing, but set nothing'. The chosen reading is defensible, but rule 7 asks for the choice to be recorded, and the reasons cite only Mrs Griffiths. (For 'trowest', Furness himself prefers Capell's 'know'; the proposal's 'believe' is the majority reading of Warburton, Schmidt and Onions, and is properly noted.)
findings.fix: No text change. Add to the reasons: 'Schmidt's alternative readings (Furness) noted; Mrs Griffiths's reading chosen.'

findings.original: And thou shalt have more / Than two tens to a score.
findings.proposed_text: and you shall have more than two tens to a score.
findings.issue: The punchline is kept word for word. Listeners do not reliably know that a score is twenty (Schmidt score 3; Onions). The joke is an impossible sum, more than twenty in every twenty, which Kent dismisses as 'nothing', and it may not land. Keeping the whore/more/score rhyme is a fair reason; a short gloss can keep both.
findings.fix: and you shall have more than two tens to a score, more than twenty in every twenty.

findings.original: e.g. 4.98, displayed line 6: 'I would fain learn to lie.'; 4.68, six displayed lines
findings.proposed_text: 4.98 unit 'lines 5–5 [I would fain learn to lie.]'; every unit of 4.68 reads 'lines 1–1'
findings.issue: The unit line numbers follow the drafter's source, LR-passages.md, which shows each prose run as one line. They do not follow the Gutenberg lineation displayed in this review packet. The exact 'o' text fixes each span, and every unit pairs corresponding content, so there is no content error.
findings.fix: Renumber the prose units against the displayed lines (e.g. make the last unit of 4.98 'lines 6–6'), or state the one-line-per-prose-run convention in the packet header.

current_defects_confirmed: 4.63–4.70: 'coxcomb' is never glossed (Schmidt coxcomb 1, a fool's cap, citing this passage; Minsheu in Furness).
4.65: 'my pretty knave' is heard as 'rogue' (Schmidt knave 1; Lear's fondness noted by Cowden Clarke and Lloyd in Furness).
4.66, 4.71, 4.74, 4.95, 4.99: 'sirrah' is left archaic.

4.68: 'smile as the wind sits' is untranslated (Schmidt, wind and sit, citing this line), 'must necessarily wear' is stilted, and the banished/blessed paradox is not audible (Capell and Moberly in Furness).
4.72: 'Lady Brach' is unexplained (Steevens in Furness: 'a bitch of the hunting kind'; Schmidt brach, citing this line). 'a dog who must to kennel' keeps the archaic ellipsis.
4.73: 'A pestilent gall to me!' is opaque or misleading today. 'gall' here means anything bitter (Schmidt gall 3, citing this line).

4.76: 'Lend less than you owe' (owe = own: Schmidt owe 2; Furness) and 'keep behind the door' (in-a-door = at home: Schmidt; Onions) are mis-glosses. 'Learn more than you trust' and 'Wager less than you throw' are opaque.
4.81–4.82: the dash after 'Please tell him' breaks the sentence, and the 'nothing' joke is under-landed.
4.86: 'presently' is a false friend, 'motley' is unglossed, and 'Or do you stand for him' is ambiguous ('tolerate').

4.90: 'won't let me' is left hanging after Kent's 'not altogether fool', which is the concrete for the abstract (Furness). 'a monopoly on it' is vague (Jennens and Warburton in Furness), and the oath 'faith' is archaic.
4.92: 'carried your ass on your back' is heard as 'backside', and 'like myself' hides 'like a fool' (Eccles in Furness).
4.94: 'grace' (favour: Johnson in Furness) and 'foppish' (foolish: Schmidt, citing this line) are untranslated, and the word order is archaic.
4.96: 'put down your own breeches' is unidiomatic. 4.98 keeps archaic inversions.
Conventions: unspaced em dashes, and mid-sentence capitals left over from the verse lineation.
current_defects_disputed: 4.70: the claim that 'all my living' now suggests earnings is overstated. 'living' in the sense of livelihood or means is still current and close to Schmidt's 'property, possession, fortune'. 'everything I own' is clearer, but the current did not mislead.
current_better: 4.71, 4.95, 4.99: 'sirrah', though archaic, kept Lear's rebuke distinct from his affectionate 'boy' (see finding).

passages.judgement: Better overall. It restores omissions ('Haply', 'for ever', 'For', the heart image, 'untender') and fixes real mis-glosses (darker, challenge, validity, interess'd, messes, neighbour'd), all soundly sourced. One change overstates Cordelia (1.36 'above all'), and a few defect claims against the current are overstated. The current's 'and most honor you' was better, and its 'blood-tie' is a defensible reading.

findings.original: to thine and Albany’s issue / Be this perpetual.
findings.proposed_text: Let this be perpetual for you and Albany's heirs.
findings.issue: This paragraph is marked keep, but spoken, 'for you and Albany's heirs' is heard as two recipients: you, and Albany's heirs. The original makes the grant perpetual to the children of Goneril and Albany together. Minor.
findings.fix: Let this be perpetual for your and Albany's heirs.

findings.issue: The exclamation mark is fine, but the reason misattributes it. Furness's 1880 text follows the First Folio ('in this edition the text of the First Folio has been virtually followed', Preface), not the Globe. The '!' is Furness's editorial punctuation; the Gutenberg source has a comma.
findings.fix: Reason: 'The exclamation follows the punctuation of the Folio-based text printed in Furness, New Variorum King Lear (1880).'

findings.original: what can you say to draw / A third more opulent than your sisters? Speak.
findings.proposed_text: what can you say to win a third more lavish than your sisters'? Speak.
findings.issue: 'opulent' (rich) is clear current English. 'lavish', kept from the current without comment, means extravagant or generously given, so it describes the gift rather than the wealth of the land.
findings.fix: what can you say to win a third more opulent than your sisters'? Speak.

findings.original: Obey you, love you, and most honour you.
findings.proposed_text: obey you, love you, and honor you above all.
findings.issue: 'most honour' is an intensifier (honour you most highly), the measured third of the duties she returns 'as are right fit'. 'above all' makes it an absolute ranking. That is the kind of total claim Cordelia refuses a few lines later, when she says half her love, care and duty will go to her husband, so the change nudges her toward her sisters' hyperbole. The reason's claim that 'most honor you' is unnatural is weak: 'most' before a verb is ordinary formal English ('I most sincerely thank you').
findings.fix: obey you, love you, and honor you most highly.

findings.original: Why have my sisters husbands if they say / They love you all? ... To love my father all.
findings.proposed_text: Why do my sisters have husbands if they say they love you completely? ... and still give all my love to my father.
findings.issue: The two 'all's answer each other, and 'all' means exclusively, with nothing left for a husband. 'completely', kept from the current, blurs that exclusivity and breaks an echo that the proposal's own last clause restores.
findings.fix: Why do my sisters have husbands if they say they give you all their love?

findings.original: For, by the sacred radiance of the sun,
findings.proposed_text: For by the sacred light of the sun,
findings.issue: 'light', kept from the current, replaces 'radiance', which is clear current English and grander. Capell (Furness) stresses the solemnity of Lear's oaths, and in an oath like this the plainer word lowers the register without making anything clearer.
findings.fix: For by the sacred radiance of the sun,

findings.proposed_text: all kinship, and every claim of blood that makes you mine.
findings.issue: This follows Schmidt (property 3, 'ownership', citing this line), which is a sound reading. But Furness also records Delius ('a stronger expression of the idea contained in propinquity') and Wright ('rising, as it were, to identity of blood'). The choice is not recorded. The current 'blood-tie' is a fair rendering of that second reading, not an omission.
findings.fix: Keep the text and record the choice in the reasons, or cover both readings: 'all kinship, and the shared blood that makes you mine.'

current_defects_confirmed: 1.20: 'deeper purpose' leans toward 'more profound', but 'darker' means more secret (Warburton in Furness), 'what has not been told before' (Johnson in Furness).

1.20: 'where nature is matched by merit' drops challenge = claim as due (Schmidt challenge vb. 1, citing this line; Steevens and Crosby in Furness). 'younger shoulders' adds an image, 'we have at this hour a settled will to publish' is stilted, 'have long been making their courting visit' is awkward, and 'son of Cornwall' is unexplained.
1.25: 'she names my very deed of love' is left untranslated (Wright, Delius and Eccles in Furness).

1.29: 'validity' is a false friend (value: Schmidt, cited in Furness). 'compete to be chosen' loses the claim in 'interess'd' (Schmidt interest 3, citing this line; Minsheu 'having right in', via Wright in Furness).
1.34: 'bond' is left bare at the crux of the scene (Schmidt bond 2, 'obligation, duty', citing this line; Eccles in Furness).
1.35: the archaic 'How now' replaces the sputtering 'How, how'.
1.36: 'Haply' is omitted, turning a hedged supposition into a prediction. 'to love my father all' is unnatural.
1.37: 'But do you mean what you say?' drops the heart image.
1.39: 'unfeeling' rewrites the clear 'untender' (Schmidt: 'unkind, ungentle', citing this line) and loses the young/tender play.

1.41: 'for ever' and the connective 'For' are omitted (Steevens in Furness: 'from this time'). 'the mysteries of Hecate' is unglossed (Schmidt: 'the goddess of hell and of sorcery', citing this line), and 'from which we exist' is unnatural. 'cannibal' is added and 'messes' dropped (Schmidt mess 1; Capell and Wright in Furness on generation = offspring). 'neighbour'd' is flattened to 'love'.
Conventions: unspaced em dashes in 1.20, 1.21, 1.25, 1.27, 1.29, 1.34, 1.36 and 1.41.
current_defects_disputed: 1.20: 'interest in territory' is not a false friend. In current English an 'interest in' land is a legal right or share in it, which is Schmidt's sense (interest 4, 'possession, property', citing this line). 'possession' is clearer by ear, but the current was not wrong.
1.20: 'publish' is at most a mild false friend, since 'make public' is a current sense. 'announce' is an improvement rather than a correction.

1.21: 'adds an image of fainting' overstates. 'makes the breath grow faint' means the breath grows weak, a fair rendering of 'makes breath poor'. The proposal is better at showing that the failure is one of expression, but the current added nothing.
1.36: 'most honor you' is not unnatural syntax. 'most' before a verb is ordinary formal English, and the proposed replacement overstates (see finding).

1.41: the claim that 'property of blood' was reduced to 'blood-tie' is disputable. 'blood-tie' matches Delius's and Wright's reading ('identity of blood', Furness); only Schmidt's 'ownership' reading is lost.
current_better: 1.36: 'and most honor you' was more accurate than the proposed 'and honor you above all'.
1.41: 'blood-tie' is a defensible reading of 'property of blood' (Delius, Wright).
